title: AI Guardrails Aren’t Stopping Criminal Hackers
gist: CrowdStrike analyzed four previously unreported threat groups (Chinese, Spanish/English, Indonesian and Russian-speaking) that used agentic AI, mostly Anthropic's Claude and Deepseek models, to run autonomous attacks between May and August, bypassing safeguards by claiming the work was authorized pen testing. Attackers favored older, cheaper models and exploited basic security hygiene gaps rather than new vulnerabilities.

insights.claim: CrowdStrike studied four previously unreported groups operating in Chinese, Spanish and English, Indonesian and Russian that used agentic AI in attacks between May and August, with the first two showing sophisticated AI harnesses.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Agentic AI is spreading to low-skill criminals, raising baseline attack volume.
insights.locator: Researchers from the threat intelligence firm CrowdStrike

insights.claim: All four actors left their AI infrastructure openly accessible on web servers, which let CrowdStrike analyze their activity and models, largely Anthropic's Claude plus open-weight Deepseek models.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Operational-security lapses are a detection opportunity for defenders.
insights.locator: All had left their AI infrastructure openly accessible

insights.claim: The Spanish and English actor compromised at least 15 Argentine health care organizations, stole credentials and medical records from at least one, and used a Supervisor Claude Code agent to direct an Executor agent with models including Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Haiku 4.5 and Deepseek V4 Pro.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Multi-agent supervisor/executor architectures are now in criminal use against health care.
insights.locator: The actor that worked in Spanish and English

insights.claim: The Chinese-speaking actor compromised government targets in Brazil and Colombia and private firms in Brazil and the US across biotech, healthcare, food and beverage, retail, technology and travel, mainly using Claude Opus 4.8 via a China-based AI proxy with fallbacks.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Proxy access and fallback routing show attackers hedge against model access being cut off.

insights.claim: The Indonesian actor, the least sophisticated, still compromised multiple Indonesian government domains and a Bangladeshi government domain using basic public skills and harnesses.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Even crude AI use yields successful government breaches.

insights.claim: All four actors circumvented AI safeguards, often by convincing models the activity was authorized penetration testing, including adding files to an agent's working directory to show tasks are approved.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Context-based authorization claims are a systemic weakness in guardrails for agentic tools.

insights.claim: The attackers used multiple models to exploit differences in guardrails, and CrowdStrike's Adam Meyers says models do not have equivalent protections even within one company.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Guardrail inconsistency across models and versions creates routing arbitrage for attackers.
insights.quote: The models don't all have equivalent guardrails and protections, even from one company
insights.locator: “The models don't all have equivalent guardrails

insights.claim: The Chinese-speaking actor used a run-time patch tool called ClawGod to add functionality to Claude Code and attempt to remove the CYBER_RISK_INSTRUCTION from its system prompt, which limits it to authorized security testing.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Client-side system-prompt tampering shows the limits of prompt-level safeguards.
insights.locator: The Chinese-speaking actor also used what's known

insights.claim: Less sophisticated actors sometimes tried to bully models with crude, aggressive prompts to accept that the activity was legitimate, while sophisticated actors built more strategic narratives.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Social-engineering of models works at multiple skill levels.
insights.locator: The more sophisticated actors were typically more strategic

themes.theme: Economics: older models and AI speed

insights.claim: Attackers mostly used older models rather than frontier ones, and Meyers says model routing and selection matters because newer models are expensive and often overkill.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Frontier model restrictions alone would not stop most malicious use; cost discipline mirrors legitimate AI usage.
insights.quote: Model routing and selection is very important because it’s expensive and a lot of times would be overkill to use newer models

insights.claim: Meyers says these attacks use no new exploits or novel vulnerabilities but exploit AI's speed and volume against preventable security hygiene issues.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Basic patching and hygiene remain the best defense against AI-scaled attacks.
insights.quote: these attacks are not using new exploits or novel vulnerabilities

insights.claim: Meyers observes that humans do initial probing and then engage AI for hacking at scale, so a human remains behind even agentic attacks.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop attribution and behavioral signatures still apply.
